title: 台風 26日にかけ警報級の大雨恐れ
body: 台風30号は26日、九州に接近する見通しです。また、前線の影響で西日本と東日本の広い範囲では25日から警報級の大雨となる恐れがあり、警戒が必要です。大型の台風30号は25日午前6時現在、東シナ海を北上しています。25日の午後には東寄りに進路を変え、26日、九州に接近する見込みです。その後は温帯低気圧に変わりながら本州付近を進むと予想されています。本州には前線が停滞していて、九州から関東では25日から26日にかけて警報級の大雨となる恐れがあります。26日朝までに予想される雨量は、九州北部で200mmなどとなっていて、その後の24時間では、四国や関東甲信で200mmの雨が予想されています。道路の冠水や河川の氾濫などに警戒してください。

title: フランス全土でデモ再び 厳戒態勢
body: フランス各地で24日、生活苦や公共サービスへの不満を理由とする大規模なデモが行われた。17日のデモには事前予測を上回る計55万人（内務省発表）が参加し、一部で暴動や略奪も発生したことから、当局は全国で7万人の警察官らを配置する厳戒態勢を敷いた。【写真】マクロン大統領=AP。｢暴動は、マクロン氏の路線が招いた帰結だ｣と東大の中山洋平教授は指摘する24日、パリで労働組合などが参加するデモの出発地点には、開始前から数百人が集結。若者らが「マクロン（大統領）辞めろ」と叫んだ。医療や教育などの公共サービスへの不満を記したメッセージボードも見られた。パリのデモに参加した大学生のアナイス・ルゲネックさん（20）は「マクロン政権は国民の声を聞いていない。ケアが必要な人、生活に苦しんでいる人が無視されている」と憤る。自身は恵まれていると話しつつ、インフレ（物価高）の影響は日々感じる。「食べる量を減らすようにした」。マクロン政権は、そうした一般市民の苦しみを十分に認識していないと感じるという。パリのレピュブリック広場では、1週間前の騒乱の爪痕がなお残り、焼け落ちた露店やひび割れたガラスがそのままになっていた。付近の店は板で外壁を補強し、貼り紙で一時休業を知らせる店舗も目立つ。■デモの制限、｢もはやフランスではない｣現地メディアによると、当局はパリで労組が申請したデモ行進のルートを認めず、中心部から離れたルートに変更した。中部リヨンでは集会の禁止区域に集まったとして、治安当局が催涙弾を使って人々を解散させたという。マクロン大統領は22日、労組以外のデモは原則として禁じると表明。都市中心部での活動も認めない方針だ。AFP通信によると、24日は全国で前週より2割多い警備要員を投入。ルーブル美術館も安全のため閉鎖された。ただ、デモの制限や警察の対応には批判が相次いでおり、フランスの環境政党のトンドリエ党首は23日、デモをする自由さえ損なわれたとして、「もう自分の国だと思えない」とラジオ番組で批判。人権擁護などに取り組む国際機関「欧州評議会」のマイケル・オフラハティ人権弁務官も23日、欧州各地で週末にデモが行われることを踏まえ、「平和的に集会する権利を保障し、警察活動が人権に適合した形で行われる」ことを求めた。フランス内務省によると、17日の騒乱に際しては、2397人が拘束され、警察官と憲兵計997人が負傷した。商業施設の被害も甚大で、政府は17、18日に「数千店」が被害を受けたと発表している。（パリ=藤原学思）

title: GMO不正接続 一瞬で119万円消失
body:
一瞬で１１９万円が――。ＧＭＯインターネットのクラウドサービスが不正アクセスを受けた問題では、ＦＸ（外国為替証拠金）取引を行う個人投資家らが、将来の蓄えや子どもの教育費などを目的に運用していた資産の一部を一夜にして失った。個人情報が公開されるリスクもあり、不安を募らせている。（村上藍、木村誠）【図解】ＧＭＯインターネットへのサイバー攻撃の構図
大阪府の会社員女性（３７）は２２日朝、スマートフォンで自身のＦＸ口座を見て頭が真っ白になった。前日には約３００万円あった残高が、約１２０万円に減っていた。
取引履歴を見ると、２２日午前０時４０分、南アフリカの通貨「ランド」を売ってユーロを買う操作が行われ、わずか一度の取引で１１９万円の損失が出ていた。自分が普段行っている取引とは桁違いで、全く身に覚えがなく、不正アクセスの被害に遭ったとすぐに確信した。
ＦＸ取引は、将来に備えて１０年ほど前に始めた。ＧＭＯインターネットが提供するＦＸ自動売買専用サービス「お名前ドットコム　デスクトップクラウド」を使うようになったのは数年前。「名前が知られた大手で、安心感があった」
だが、コツコツと増やしてきた資金は一瞬で半分以下に減った。資産が減った場合に自動で決済される取引なども含めると、損失額は計１７８万円に上る。
同社は２４日、利用者が被った損害について補償する方針を発表したが、「問い合わせに対して何も返信がない」と不信感を募らせる。「私のような一般の利用者が安心して使えるよう、国や事業者は今回の問題に誠実に向き合って対応してほしい」と訴えた。
埼玉県草加市の会社員男性（３２）は２４日未明、そんなメールを受け取り「自分にも来たか……」と不安を募らせた。男性も２２日未明に不正取引されて約５５万円を失っていた。
メールは日本語で「不正アクセスしたハッキングチーム」を名乗り、「ＧＭＯ側に対し、返答がない場合は明日、顧客データを公開すると通告しました。このデータには、皆様の個人情報が含まれています」などと書かれていた。不正に取得したとするデータの一部も「証拠」として添付されていた。

title: 斧で殴打し殺人未遂疑い 男を逮捕
body: ２５日未明、大阪市中央区の店舗で、会社員の男が男性の頭部を斧で殴打し殺害しようとしたとして逮捕されました。【ウラドリ】「ママ会いたい」密室での取り調べで自白を迫る執拗な言葉　１６歳の少女が身に覚えのない逮捕、１８日間の拘束　その後衰弱死　一体何が･･･？２５日、殺人未遂の疑いで現行犯逮捕されたのは、大阪市浪速区に住む会社員の男（４６）です。警察によりますと男は２５日午前１時半ごろ、大阪市中央区西心斎橋にある店舗で、生野区に住む職業不詳の男性（４４）の頭部を斧で殴打し、殺害しようとした疑いがもたれています。通報を受け駆けつけた警察官により、男は現行犯逮捕されたということです。殴られた男性はけがをし、病院に搬送されています。（このニュースは最新の情報が入り次第更新されます）

title: 「Used in Japan」世界注目 なぜ
body:
日本製品を指す「Made in Japan（メイド・イン・ジャパン）」ではなく、日本で使われたものを意味する「Used in Japan（ユーズド・イン・ジャパン）」が世界で注目を集めています。この言葉は日本で大切に扱われてきた古着・リユース品のこと。丁寧に物を扱う日本人ならではの、状態のよさが海外で高評価されているのです。ユーズド品を扱う日本系ショップも、丁寧な管理、確かな評価・鑑定などが信頼を得ています。なぜ今、日本の古着やリユース品が世界で選ばれているのでしょうか。その理由と今後の可能性を探ります。
好調のブランド古着「ラグタグ」平野社長に聞く次の一手　“ユーズド・イン・ジャパン”を追い風にアジア本格攻勢出典：WWDJAPAN.com　2026/10/6(火)
外国人の間で「日本の古着」が絶賛されている明快な理由…《ユーズドインジャパン》が世界的に評価される時代に出典：マネー現代　2026/4/19(日)
Vintage Shop Guide／GOOD REGULARS グッドレギュラーがいつもある。出典：POPEYE　2025/12/28(日)
古着はミックスコーデがおすすめ！おしゃれな着こなしのコツをプロに聞く出典：読売新聞オンライン　2025/12/4(木)
これまで日本製品の高品質をうたってきた「Made in Japan」は主に新品の工業製品を指す言葉でした。一方、今のリユース市場でほめ言葉になっている「Used in Japan」は中古の衣料品が主役。腕時計や宝飾品も含みます。
「Made」と異なるのは、日本製品とは限らない点です。海外ブランドであっても、日本で大切に扱われ、好ましい状態に保たれてきた古着やバッグ、時計などが評価されています。つまり、日本人の「物持ち」のよさが国際的に好評を得ているという構図です。
商品コンディションのよさに加え、評価・鑑定力、丁寧な状態説明・梱包なども「UiJ」の魅力です。とりわけ値付けのリーズナブル感は国際的に見て「割安」と受け取られているよう。「グッドレギュラー」といわれる1980、90年代の良状態物が多いのも人気の理由です。
日本にはバブル期にあたる80～90年代に消費者が買い込んだデザイナーズ物の古着がたくさん眠っています。当時の購入世代が年齢を重ね、愛用品を手放す人は今後、増えると見込まれます。つまり、上質の「Used in Japan」はさらに流通量が増える流れにあり、この先も世界で人気が高まっていきそうです。

title: 中国で首相と会談 正恩氏日帰りか
body: 北朝鮮の金正恩総書記が中国を訪問し、李強首相と会談したことが確認されたと、韓国の情報当局が明らかにしました。韓国政府関係者によりますと、金総書記は15日に開通した北朝鮮と中国を結ぶ「新鴨緑江大橋」を通って中国に入ったとされます。金総書記は、遼寧省の丹東を訪問したとみられ、中国の李強首相と会談したということです。丹東では一部地域で交通規制が敷かれたほか、朝鮮戦争での中国・北朝鮮の共闘の歴史を伝える記念館では25日の予約が取れず、新鴨緑江大橋周辺のホテルでも予約が取りづらくなっています。25日は中国が朝鮮戦争に参戦した日で、金総書記が記念行事に出席するか注目されますが、韓国の情報当局は金総書記が24日中に帰国する可能性が高いとみています。

title: 正恩氏が電撃訪中 開通の大橋通り
body:
【ソウル聯合ニュース】北朝鮮の金正恩（キム・ジョンウン）国務委員長（朝鮮労働党総書記）が24日、中国を訪問したことが確認された。金氏の訪中はおよそ1年ぶり。韓国政府の消息筋は聯合ニュースに対し、金氏が今月15日に正式に開通した新鴨緑江大橋を通って中国の遼寧省・丹東に到着したと明らかにした。トランプ米大統領が年内の米朝首脳会談を目指すなか、金氏が11月のアジア太平洋経済協力会議（APEC）首脳会議を前に電撃的に訪中したことから、注目される。最近、「金正恩氏が死亡した」との情報が国内外のSNSで拡散したが、今回の訪中で健在ぶりもアピールすることになる。

title: 露は「人質外交」解放の米紙記者
body:
【ニューヨーク共同】ロシア当局にスパイ容疑で16カ月以上拘束後に解放された米紙ウォールストリート・ジャーナルのエバン・ゲルシコビッチ記者は23日、北海道新聞記者の拘束は「ロシアの人質外交であることが明白だ」と述べロシアを批判した。記者解放にはロシア側が求める何らかの条件交渉が必要で、日本政府には同盟国などとの協力が欠かせないとの認識を示した。米ニューヨークでの講演会後、共同通信の取材に応じた。【写真】「ロシア兵器9割に日本部品」　ミサイルや無人機に転用　名指しされた日本企業13社
ゲルシコビッチ氏は日ロ関係が悪化する中「ロシアは日本人を拘束しても構わない」と考えた可能性があると指摘した。

title: モンゴル火災 当局が賠償請求検討
body: 【北京時事】モンゴル東部ドルノド県で今月上旬、自然保護区を含む大規模な草原火災が発生したことを受け、同国政府は24日までに閣議を開き、責任者を特定した上で、被害の賠償請求を検討する方針を示した。【写真】KDDIの松田浩路社長モンゴル国営放送などが報じた。ノムトイバヤル副首相は「謝罪の言葉だけでは済まない」と述べたという。草原火災は、モンゴルで通信事業を展開するKDDIの子会社「モビコム」の日本人幹部らが車列で移動中に発生した。KDDIは23日に謝罪声明を発表。当局の調査に全面的に協力する考えを示す一方、「社員が法令違反行為を行っていないことを確認している」と説明した。

title: 裁量労働制 乱用防止へ労使が一致
body: 実際に働いた時間ではなく、あらかじめ一定時間働いたとみなす「裁量労働制」をめぐり、労働政策審議会（厚生労働相の諮問機関）で23日、見直しに向けた具体的な議論が始まった。制度の乱用を防ぐため、長時間労働になった場合に裁量労働制の適用を外す措置の必要性について労働側、使用者（経営）側は一致した。制度の対象拡大には労働側が反対した。【写真】「つながらない権利」も議論労政審では、労働側、使用者側の委員と、有識者による公益委員が、労働基準法改正を議論している。裁量労働制について（1）乱用を防ぐ措置（2）制度の対象のあり方を議論した。

title: タイムズカー情報流出 集団訴訟へ
body: カーシェアリングサービス「タイムズカー」による情報漏えいの被害者側の弁護士は23日、サービスを展開する貸し駐車場大手「パーク24」側に集団訴訟を起こす意向を明らかにした。パーク24が示した運転免許証の画像データ流出に対する見舞金3000円が低額だとし、適正な金額の損害賠償を求めるとしている。【写真で見る】タイムズカーのユーザーに届いたメールの文面東京弁護士会所属の牧野裕貴弁護士は9月末に集団訴訟に向けた専用サイトを開設。23日時点で約9万人が登録したという。被害者からの正式な委任手続きを進める。提訴の時期や原告数は未定とした。牧野弁護士は「タイムズカー側は個人情報を適切に管理する義務を怠り精神的損害を与えた。2次被害防止の手間や、なりすましの危険性を考慮すると見舞金の金額は不十分だ」と述べた。パーク24は23日、氏名や住所、メールアドレス、運転免許情報など662万8007件の情報漏えいが確認されたとする調査結果を公表。運転免許証の画像データなど本人確認情報の漏えいが確認された約146万件については、画像データへのアクセスや外部送信を示す痕跡が確認された被害者に1人あたり3000円を支払う方針を示した。【安達恒太郎】

title: OKURA不適切還付 追徴額5.8億円
body:
高級腕時計の中古品販売を手がける「OKURA」（東京都豊島区）が、消費税の免税制度で計約5億円の不適切な還付を受けたと東京国税局から指摘されていたことが24日、関係者への取材で分かった。指摘期間は2025年7月までの約4年間で、追徴額は過少申告加算税を含め約5億8千万円に上るという。【写真】訪日客の免税、出国時返金に変更　「転売ヤー」対策で11月から
同社は取材に「国税局と一部見解の相違が生じる結果となったことを真摯に受け止め、管理体制の強化に努める」とコメントしている。関係者によると、OKURAはブローカーが手配した「買い子」と呼ばれる外国人らと多数回にわたり取引。消費税分を除いた免税価格で高級腕時計を販売していた。消費税はモノやサービスを売ったときに受け取る税額より、仕入れで支払った税額が多い場合にその差額が還付される。同社は免税売り上げとして税務署に申告し、仕入れにかかった消費税分の還付を受けていたが、買い子は購入した腕時計を別の人に譲渡したとみられ、東京国税局は免税要件を満たしていないと判断したもようだ。

title: 「Used in Japan」世界注目 なぜ
body:
日本製品を指す「Made in Japan（メイド・イン・ジャパン）」ではなく、日本で使われたものを意味する「Used in Japan（ユーズド・イン・ジャパン）」が世界で注目を集めています。この言葉は日本で大切に扱われてきた古着・リユース品のこと。丁寧に物を扱う日本人ならではの、状態のよさが海外で高評価されているのです。ユーズド品を扱う日本系ショップも、丁寧な管理、確かな評価・鑑定などが信頼を得ています。なぜ今、日本の古着やリユース品が世界で選ばれているのでしょうか。その理由と今後の可能性を探ります。
好調のブランド古着「ラグタグ」平野社長に聞く次の一手　“ユーズド・イン・ジャパン”を追い風にアジア本格攻勢出典：WWDJAPAN.com　2026/10/6(火)
外国人の間で「日本の古着」が絶賛されている明快な理由…《ユーズドインジャパン》が世界的に評価される時代に出典：マネー現代　2026/4/19(日)
Vintage Shop Guide／GOOD REGULARS グッドレギュラーがいつもある。出典：POPEYE　2025/12/28(日)
古着はミックスコーデがおすすめ！おしゃれな着こなしのコツをプロに聞く出典：読売新聞オンライン　2025/12/4(木)
これまで日本製品の高品質をうたってきた「Made in Japan」は主に新品の工業製品を指す言葉でした。一方、今のリユース市場でほめ言葉になっている「Used in Japan」は中古の衣料品が主役。腕時計や宝飾品も含みます。
「Made」と異なるのは、日本製品とは限らない点です。海外ブランドであっても、日本で大切に扱われ、好ましい状態に保たれてきた古着やバッグ、時計などが評価されています。つまり、日本人の「物持ち」のよさが国際的に好評を得ているという構図です。
商品コンディションのよさに加え、評価・鑑定力、丁寧な状態説明・梱包なども「UiJ」の魅力です。とりわけ値付けのリーズナブル感は国際的に見て「割安」と受け取られているよう。「グッドレギュラー」といわれる1980、90年代の良状態物が多いのも人気の理由です。
日本にはバブル期にあたる80～90年代に消費者が買い込んだデザイナーズ物の古着がたくさん眠っています。当時の購入世代が年齢を重ね、愛用品を手放す人は今後、増えると見込まれます。つまり、上質の「Used in Japan」はさらに流通量が増える流れにあり、この先も世界で人気が高まっていきそうです。

title: 大阪IR ディーラー人材確保に課題
body:
大阪市で2030年秋ごろの開業を目指すカジノを含む統合型リゾート施設（IR）は、ゲームを進行するディーラーの人材確保が課題となりそうだ。ディーラー育成の民間機関「日本カジノスクール」は、IR運営事業者のMGM大阪と連携し、公認コースを東京と大阪に新設する。最大3000人が必要とみられるIR開業までに2000人の育成を目標とするが、受講者を十分に集められるかが鍵となる。【ひと目で分かる】ギャンブル等依存症の若年化深刻　借金の平均額、過去最多にIRは市内の人工島・夢洲（ゆめしま）に設置。大阪府は経済波及効果を毎年1兆1400億円と見込み、施設全体の売り上げの8割をカジノで稼ぐ計画だ。効果を享受するには、ディーラーを始めとする関連サービス業の人材確保と受け入れ態勢の整備が欠かせない。ディーラーの雇用人数は公表されていないが、日本カジノスクールは、ポーカーなどのテーブルゲームを470台設置する計画や24時間営業の交代制などを踏まえ、最大3000人のディーラー需要を想定している。公認コースは27年春に設置し、初年度の定員は東京・大阪で計800人を予定する。スクールの大岩根成悦校長は「（開業の）30年を待つのではなく、今からIRを見据えた準備を進める。世界へ羽ばたく人材を育て、IRの成功に貢献したい」と意気込んでいる。授業はMGMのトレーニングを受けた講師らが担当する。受講期間は3カ月～1年で、学費は教材費や入学金で約60万円。ルーレットやバカラなどの実技実習に加え、不正防止や現金管理、ギャンブル依存症対策などを履修する。修了生はMGM大阪の採用試験で書類選考が免除され、実技オーディションに進める。プロになった場合の日本での年収は明確になっていないが、平均400万円程度との見方もある。海外では、チップを含めて1000万円以上というケースもみられる。一方、IR開業まで約4年あることや国内での勤務先が限られることなどから、受講者が想定通りに集まらない懸念もある。ギャンブル社会学に詳しい大阪商業大の谷岡一郎学長は「IRはこれからの日本を変えていく産業だ。人材育成では、法律や経営に関する知識も身に付ける必要がある」と指摘する。計画通りに人材を育成するには、MGM大阪が求める技術を備えた人材を安定して輩出する指導体制に加え、ギャンブル依存症への懸念や社会的偏見を払拭するための教育環境の整備も課題だ。
IR整備法では全国で最大3区域の整備が認められており、北海道や愛知県などでも誘致の動きがある。（香西広豊）

title: Almost 1,000 arrested as clashes follow another day of mass protests across France
summary: Officials have so far managed to avoid a repeat of last weekend's rioting and looting as hundreds of thousands took part in demonstrations.
body:
Watch: BBC in Paris as police charge protesters during skirmishes
Nearly 1,000 arrests were made as hundreds of thousands of people took part in another day of protests across France which were followed by some clashes late on Saturday, officials have said.
After a day of largely peaceful demonstrations, police fired tear gas and water cannon to disperse protesters in a number of cities including Paris, while barricades were set alight in Marseille and people ripped boards from a shop in Bordeaux.
But officials have so far managed to avoid rioting and looting on the scale seen last weekend, which resulted in some of the worst scenes of disorder in France's modern history.
The interior ministry said an estimated 410,000 people protested on Saturday, while the unions put the number at about 800,000.
Katya Adler: France divided over who to blame for riots and what to learn from them
Some 70,000 police officers were deployed and restrictions imposed in several cities to prevent the latest protests over the cost of living and poor school conditions from descending into the kind of chaos which saw officers outnumbered, hundreds of businesses looted and buildings torched.
President Emmanuel Macron had decreed earlier this week that only demonstrations organised by a recognised trade unions would be permitted. Hundreds of people have been jailed for vandalism, arson and looting after fast-track court hearings in recent days.
In the southern port of Marseille, protesters erected makeshift street barricades and set them alight late on Saturday
Clashes between protesters and riot police in Paris erupted at the end of a peaceful march from the city's Porte d'Italie towards Porte de Vincennes on Saturday, where the police operation included an elite unit that usually deals with organised crime and counter-terrorism.
Some protesters were seen erecting makeshift barricades and pelting officers with projectiles, while police baton-charged groups of masked youths who were smashing the windows of a car dealership.
French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said that "several thousand radical activists gathered at the rear of the march, including around 500 individuals identified as rioters", the AFP news agency reported.
Protesters clash with police at a demonstration in Bordeaux
In the southern port of Marseille, rubbish bins were set ablaze and metal sheets used to block streets. A law enforcement vehicle was seen driving through a burning barricade in France's second-largest city.
Meanwhile, some protesters in dark clothing and face coverings were seen taking boards off a building to build a street barricade in the southern city of Bordeaux.
In Lyon, police used tear gas grenades to disperse a crowd which had reportedly gathered in an area deemed off-limits by the local prefecture.
"There were around 150 of us, mostly secondary school and university students. Then the tear gas came almost immediately. You could barely see anything in the street," said one protester in France's third-largest city.
Nuñez said late in the day that nearly 1,000 people had been arrested, a number he said would increase.
The minister also said two people had been "seriously injured": one in the south-western city of Toulouse, and another one in Clermont-Ferrand, central France.
"We really want a change in France," a teenage protester told the BBC
Earlier, a peaceful protester in Paris who gave her name as Zelie told the BBC people had taken to the streets because they were "really frustrated" and had been "suffering a lot" since Macron came to office.
"They keep us quiet. They take our money, they tax us a lot and we can't say anything. Today we are in the streets because it's been too long, it's been too much," the 26-year-old said.
Two masked teenage protesters, who did not want to give their names, also said their generation was in despair and felt abandoned by the government.
"I think looting is really not good," one of the demonstrators said of last Saturday's disorder. "But it's because of poverty and the violence of the police."
He added that the protests would end "when we have a response to our demands. We really want a change in France".
Meanwhile, some 13,000 people joined a rally against the hard-right National Rally party in the north-central city of Orléans which proceeded peacefully.
Mass protests triggered by similar issues as in France also rocked several other European cities on Saturday.
In Albania's capital Tirana, riot police fired tear gas to disperse thousands of anti-government demonstrators, while clashes were also reported in Belgium's capital Brussels.
In Milan, northern Italy, a major security operation including hundreds of soldiers alongside police prevented protesters gathering in the city. Many had feared a repeat of violent scenes last week when some started fires, smashed windows and looted shops.
Around 550,000 people took part in last weekend's demonstrations against rising fuel prices and the cost of living, with frustrations escalating after weeks of student protests. The chaos which followed resulted in more than 2,500 arrests.
Marches were initially largely peaceful but became marred by scenes of violence, looting and destruction, with more than 2,000 shops and other businesses across France said to have been directly impacted. The damage was estimated "at hundreds of millions euros", France's Chambers of Commerce and Industry (CCI) said.
One demonstrator's hand was blown off by a police crowd-control grenade, according to the AFP news agency, while about 1,000 police officers were injured.
The French authorities later said they were forced to impose overnight curfews in Paris and other cities.
The continuing protests come ahead of France's presidential elections in six months' time, andleading contenders have levelled the blameat Macron and his ministers.

title: Ukraine says Starlink connection 'now stable' after network limits
summary: The slowed Starlink connections had affected the Ukraine's military and drone operations for a week.
body:
Ukraine's military uses the network of 10,000 low Earth orbit satellites extensively for military operations
Ukraine now has a "stable connection" to Starlink, its defence minister has said, after its military suffered days of restricted connectivity on the satellite internet network.
Kyiv relies on the Starlink and its military-grade counterpart Starshield for piloting drones and operations within Ukraine, but last week accused US President Donald Trump of telling owner Elon Musk to place limits on it.
This meant drones would lose connection when travelling at 161km/h (100mph) or more, it said. Trump denied doing so before saying Musk had "put it back".
Defence Minister Yevhenii Khmara said that speeds of more than 400km/h were now possible on the network, indicating that full capability had been restored.
"This result is above all important for our front, for our soldiers, for the operation of drones, for logistics and for communications," he said in a statement on Saturday.
Ukraine's military uses the network of 10,000 low Earth orbit satellites extensively for military operations, particularly in remote areas on the battlefield.
Ukraine uses both the civilian service Starlink and the more secure Starshield, which Musk said was controlled by the US military when he suggested the Pentagon could be behind the recent issues.
Russia is not authorised to use Starlink, so when Ukraine sends long-range missiles or drones deep into Russia to hit oil refineries, the network does not work.
The debacle over Starlink began last week, and emerged during a broader diplomatic row between Trump and his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky over Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil infrastructure.
Faced with midterm elections next month, Trump has waived some sanctions on Russia and agreed a deal to import Russian diesel for the US market - a move criticised by Ukraine and its European allies.
Trump said the strikes on Russian oil refineries, which Kyiv says are crucial to stemming the main revenue source for Moscow's war effort, have pushed global prices higher.
While the attacks have had an impact on global fuel prices, rises seen this year haveprimarily been due to the Iran war.
Zelensky said that, as well as seemingly limiting Starlink capability in Ukraine, the US had also threatened to withdraw intelligence sharing if the strikes did not stop, something Trump also denied.
Meanwhile, fighting on the ground continues.
Russia's ministry of defence wrote on Telegram on Saturday that their air defences shot down 616 Ukrainian fixed-wing drones, striking a number of regions across the country, includingRussian-annexed Crimea.
Sergey Aksyonov, the region's Moscow-backed governor, said restrictions on electricity and water had been put in place because of power cuts caused by the drone strike.
Meanwhile, Ukrainian authorities said they struck a missile component manufacturer, a chemical plant and an aircraft at a military airfield inside Russia in the past 24 hours.
They also said that Russia carried out 88 air strikes using 309 glide bombs and 10,270 kamikaze drones on Friday.

title: Palestinian families displaced as Israeli forces demolish Hebron homes
summary: The crackdown follows the killing of two Israeli soldiers by two Palestinian gunmen on Friday - and comes just days ahead of Israel's election.
body:
More than 200 families have been displaced, Palestinian officials say
The Israeli military has launched a sweeping crackdown in the occupied West Bank, demolishing homes and businesses in the city of Hebron and displacing hundreds of families, according to local officials.
Footage shared online showed destruction caused by Israeli bulldozers, with at least one whole street appearing to have been flattened. The military has also cordoned off the city, heavily restricting the movement of its 200,000 residents.
The operation was announced by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Friday, in response to the killing of two Israeli soldiers by two Palestinian gunmen in an attack on a checkpoint. Three other Israeli soldiers were injured, and the gunmen were also killed.
Netanyahu said on Friday that buildings around the site of the attack and the neighbourhoods that the two gunmen were from would be "destroyed".
Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz said about 2,000 residents had been displaced by the operation, which centred on the Ein Deir Baha and Farsh al-Hawa neighbourhoods, and targeted homes, businesses, industrial sites and infrastructure.
He said dozens of families had been forced to spend the night outside, with some told to leave without taking their vehicles, while homes were marked for demolition with spray paint.
He added that he believed the military planned to displace a total of 2,500 people from about 0.35 sq km of urban land. The city's governor and deputy mayor meanwhile said at least 200 families had been displaced.
The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) did not respond immediately to the BBC's request for comment. It said in a statement on social media that it had dozens of targets across the West Bank and that its operations would last for several days.
Wreckage was seen around the site of Friday's shooting following demolitions by Israeli forces
Bulldozers began demolitions on Friday afternoon
Photos of one of the suspected gunmen in Friday's attack were shared by AFP news agency
It is common practice for Israeli forces to demolish the homes of Palestinians who are suspected of carrying out attacks on Israelis in the West Bank - a practice Israeli rights groups have criticised as collective punishment.
Netanyahu likened the operation to previous operations in Palestinian refugee camps in the north of the territory, when the Israeli military demolished hundreds of homes and displaced tens of thousands in 2025.
Friday's shooting came during a tense time for the region, with Israel's general election taking place in four days' time.
Netanyahu - who has built his campaign on the promise of security - cancelled his party's campaign events for Friday morning and headed to Hebron, wearing protective armour and posting a video on social media from the scene.
"We will evacuate the residents, go house to house, remove the weapons we find there, and deal with and destroy all terrorist infrastructure," he said.
He also announced he had reviewed plans for the largest military operation in the West Bank since 1967 - though did not say when it could be carried out. It is not clear whether the ongoing Hebron operation forms part of that.
In an interview with Israel's i24 television channel released on Saturday, he threatened "a very big surprise" for the Palestinian Authority (PA), which governs parts of the territory.
In a statement, the PA called for "urgent international action that went beyond condemnation" to prevent further forced displacement.
Meanwhile, his far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich called for Israel to launch a campaign in the West Bank "exactly like in Gaza or Lebanon," while far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir called for Israel to dismantle the PA.
Speaking to journalists, Hebron Mayor Youssef al-Jaabari said the operation was "driven by the elections," and that Netanyahu and his ministers were attempting to secure the votes of the far-right and the settlers.

title: Man arrested after fire at Hitler's mountaintop Eagle's Nest retreat
summary: Some 200 emergency personnel were deployed to fight the blaze at the Nazi dictator's Alpine residence in Germany.
body:
Watch as fire engulfs Hitler's mountaintop retreat
Police in the southern German state of Bavaria have detained a 33-year-old German manduring a fire at Adolf Hitler's Alpine mountain retreat, the Kehlsteinhaus, also known as the Eagle's Nest.
Dispatchers in Traunstein received a fire alarm from the building at 21:15 local time (19:15 GMT) on Friday and firefighters found it engulfed in flames.
Some 200 emergency personnel were deployed to the scene where the blaze was still burning early on Saturday, as police said difficult terrain hindered efforts to bring the fire under control.
Police said they apprehended the man riding a motorcyclenear the scene, German media reported. A criminal investigation has been launched.
There is currently nothing to suggest the involvement of further suspects, police official Gerhart Holzinger told a press conference on Saturday afternoon.
Public prosecutor Rainer Vietze said a psychiatric report had concluded the 33-year-old man showed signs of possible mental illness and diminished responsibility might therefore be assumed.
Vietze said a possible political motive was also being considered, but stressed the investigation was in its early stages.
The residence, above the town of Berchtesgaden, was one of several buildings in the area used by the Nazi dictator and his entourage during World War Two.
Hitler and top Nazi officials used his nearby Berghof residence to plan the invasion of the USSR in 1941 and the whole complex was considered one of his headquarters.
He also used the area as a backdrop for propaganda films portraying him as a lover of animals and nature.
Local media reported that site had been "largely destroyed" and the public was urged to avoid the area.
Bavaria's Interior Minister Joachim Herrmann told reporters that the site would "under no circumstances remain a ruin", broadcaster BR24 reported. "It is important that we continue our work of remembrance," he added.
The retreat was seen smouldering on Saturday morning
Completed by the Nazis in 1938, the Eagle's Nest, which sits at an elevation of around 1,800m (5,900ft), escaped destruction after their defeat in 1945.
Since then, it has become a popular tourist destination and houses a mountain inn.
It serves as "a cautionary reminder of the abysses of the inhumane Nazi dictatorship", according to its officialwebsite,external.
During WW2, Hitler and his followers were responsible for the deaths of tens of millions of people, including the mass murder of European Jews. Homosexuals, gypsies, the disabled and ethnic minorities were sent to concentration camps and put to death.
There has been a wider debate in Germany and Vienna over whether to preserve, repurpose or demolish buildings connected to Hitler.
While some say these buildings should be preserved for historical reasons, others have raised concerns that they could be used as monuments or places of pilgrimage for neo-Nazis and far-right extremists.
In June, Berlin authorities announced they would tear down one of Hitler's bunkers - described at the time as "the power centre of Nazi Germany" - to build flats and offices on the site.
Those critical of the plans said the bunker had "significant historical value" and that it should have been turned into a museum and memorial site with an exhibit about the end of the war.
And in July, after years of controversy, Austrian authorities refurbished the house in the town of Braunau am Inn in which Hitler was born and turned it into a police station.

title: Father who killed Oregon school gunman describes anguish over children he couldn't save
summary: Kaylub Giamanco has been hailed as a hero for killing a teenager who fatally shot three children and a teacher.
body:
Watch: Bystander who stopped Oregon school shooter describes how he approached gunman
A father who fatally shot a gunman at his daughters' school in the US state of Oregon has described his anguish over being unable to save more pupils after "hearing children pleading for their lives".
Three students and a teacher were killed by a 16-year-old former student at Silver Rail Elementary School earlier this month. The attacker was then killed by Kaylub Giamanco.
"I want to apologise for not saving their babies," Giamanco, who has been hailed as a hero, said of his thoughts for the parents of the children killed, in an interview with  Oregon Public Broadcasting (OPB) that aired on Friday.
"The gratitude for saving people's children is awesome, but there were ones that I didn't save."
Giamanco, 36, said he wanted to meet the victims' families and "cry with them and hold them".
He credited a teacher who fought the attacker with giving him the chance to intervene without losing his own life.
"I would love to give her a hug because that's a real true hero," he said.
The students who were killed were all boys, aged five, eight and 11. They were among six people in total who were shot in a classroom at the school, police said. Alongside the teacher who was killed, another child and a teacher were wounded.
Giamanco told OPB that the day of the attack began with breakfast and making packed lunches. He and his wife had spent extra time getting their daughters ready because it was school picture day.
The carpenter had taken lunch to work but decided to go home to eat with his wife instead. That decision brought him past the school as the attack began.
He initially wondered whether someone carrying a long gun was playing a prank. Then he saw him fire at a pickup truck and head towards the school.
Giamanco retrieved a handgun from his vehicle and called emergency services.
"I said, 'I'm sorry, I have to go in. People are going to die'," he told the broadcaster.
He followed the attacker, who shot through the school's locked glass doors. Hearing children pleading for their lives and more gunfire, Giamanco crawled towards the building.
"I told myself this is probably the last thing that I'm ever going to do," he said.

Police said the teacher who confronted the attacker had thrown her phone at him, tackled him and fought to take his shotgun. Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said she "almost certainly helped prevent more bloodshed".
The youngest victim was Rhoam Summer, aged five. His father said the family was "broken and lost".
Megan Lambert, 25, the teacher who was killed, was working in what her family described as her "dream job".
"She always fought for the underdog and those with special needs," they said.
The other two boys have not been publicly named at their families' request.
The injured teacher has been named as Becky Drury, 54. She said in a statement shared with US mediathat the gunman shot her as she tried to shut her classroom door.

Giamanco's name became public less than a day after the shooting. His mother, Kenda Freeman, read a family statement saying he was not seeking recognition and asking for privacy.
Shortly after the attack, Oregon Governor Tina Kotek praised his intervention while acknowledging its emotional cost.
"Your actions carry a heavy emotional burden, and I just want you to know that my thoughts are with you as well," she said.
Giamanco told OPB he now lies awake after his family goes to bed, replaying the attack.
"I relive, I see faces, I hear voices, I hear screams."

title: Rosebank: Life on the oil field at the centre of a political storm
summary: Scotland editor James Cook finds out what life is like on board a ship in an untapped oil field awaiting its fate.
body:
When we landed by helicopter at Rosebank, this oil field was at the centre of a political storm - and set to be in the path of a real one.
We arrived on Wednesday morning, just a few hours after the UK government had granted consent for the production of gas from the Jackdaw field in the North Sea.
But already attention was shifting to this wild and windy patch of the North Atlantic – the next big decision for Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh.
Rosebank is bigger than Jackdaw, it would generate higher greenhouse gas emissions, and it could be far more lucrative for its owners, Adura and Ithaca.
Nicola Boyd loves her job on the Petrojarl Rosebank vessel
This summer, along with a camera crew, I travelled to Jackdaw, 150 miles east of Aberdeen.
Now we were the first journalists to visit Rosebank.
We came here - days before Storm Boelo arrived with strong winds and heavy rain - to scrutinise a controversial project which is at the heart of a national debate about climate change, energy policy and the economy.
But we also hoped for a rare glimpse into life offshore.
"It's good fun, it's interesting, every day can change," said Nicola Boyd, who runs the helideck, and greeted us as we struggled out of our lifejackets and survival suits.
Boyd has worked offshore for nearly a decade, including a year on Rosebank - where she spends two weeks at a time followed by three weeks' leave.
"It's a job I love," she added.
The Petrojarl Rosebank is moored in the North Atlantic waiting to see if production gets the go-ahead from the UK government
It's also a job that calls for steady legs and a strong stomach.
Unlike the fixed Jackdaw platform, this installation – 80 miles north west of Shetland – is a large ship, a floating production, storage and offloading vessel (FPSO) named the Petrojarl Rosebank.
It's been chartered by the field's owners from Aberdeen-based Altera and, during my 48 hours on board, it was constantly but gently rolling on the North Atlantic swell.
Those conditions may be misleading.
With the understatement typical of an Orkney islander, lead mechanical technician Ewan Leonard told me the winter weather could be "a bit of a challenge."
"Last week we had a 30m heave coming through," he said, referring to the swell, "so we'll probably suffer more of that as the winter goes on."
Altera CEO Chris Brett told me that in the industry the environment west of Shetland is considered "as harsh as you get anywhere in the world."
Whatever your view on that industry, the sheer scale of what humans have achieved in such conditions is impressive.
Ewan Leonard says the winter weather can be "a bit of a challenge"
The deep reserves of skill, ingenuity and engineering prowess among the 122 people on board are obvious.
The jobs are well-paid and, according to Ewan Leonard, the facilities are excellent.
"We have single-man cabins, there's good gym facilities, there's a lot of rec rooms here."
Douglas Hogge, a production supervisor in charge of a team responsible for the safe extraction of oil and gas, agrees.
"There's the gym, the sauna," he said, adding "you can obviously go and get some fresh air. There's plenty of fresh air out there."
There's even a cinema.
Food on board the ship was described as "fantastic"
"As you've seen yourself, the food is fantastic on board, so no complaints." added Leonard.
Everyone we spoke to agreed with that, praising the talented chefs who sent out all sorts of delicious dishes, from braised ox cheek to mackerel to pork loin, day and night.
As dusk gathers and the nightshift get ready for work with a strange breakfast of fillet steak and chocolate brownie pudding, the vessel begins to glow in the gloom.
It is a strange sight, the decks criss-crossed by a bewilderingly complex array of pipes, valves and bright yellow steelwork.
The ship is an array of pipes, valves and bright yellow steelwork
The ship doesn't move far, rotating around a fixed central point called the turret to face into the weather, making life a little easier for those on board.
If production is approved, oil and gas will be pumped up through the turret from wells in the field below, which contains an estimated 300m to 500m barrels, enough for perhaps 25 years.
"For myself and a lot of the guys, that would see us out to retirement," said Douglas Hogge.
"We need to see this approved," he added.
Environmental campaigners strongly disagree. They've been trying to stop Rosebank for years, with some success.
"The future of the energy sector in the UK is renewable energy," said Tessa Khan, executive director of the campaigning group Uplift.
Consent for production at Rosebank was first grantedunder the Conservative government in 2023.
But in 2025, after a challenge by Greenpeace and Uplift,the Court of Session in Edinburgh ruled the approvals of the UK's largest known untapped oil field and Jackdaw were unlawfulbecause they had failed to take into account the climate impact of actually burning the fossil fuels in cars, homes and factories.
The judge, Lord Ericht, said the fields' developers could carry on with work short of producing oil and gas while they provided more detailed environmental assessments for the government and regulators to consider.
"We think Rosebank would be a disastrous decision and a terrible deal for ordinary people across this country," said Khan, urging prime minister Andy Burnham to prioritise renewables in his quest to re-industrialise the nation.
"If the government's interested in building investor confidence, giving the green light to a major new oil field is going to do the opposite," she argued.
Whatever happens with Rosebank and Jackdaw, the long-term trend for the industry is clear and it is one of decline.
It's a quarter of a century since oil production peaked and in recent yearsjobs in oil and gas have been disappearing much faster than they're being created in renewable energysuch as wind and solar power.
The oil from Rosebank would be loaded onto tankers via a gigantic hose and nozzle, which looks like the super-sized pump of an enormous floating filling station.
From there it would be sold on the international market and, most likely, taken to continental Europe for refining.
Opponents say that proves the project is of little benefit to the UK and should be rejected.
Supporters argue that's not the case because UK and European energy markets are co-dependent, adding that Rosebank will generate millions in tax for the Treasury.
Neil McCulloch, chief executive of Adura – which owns 80% of Rosebank and is a joint venture between Shell and the Norwegian state energy firm, Equinor – is optimistic.
He points out that Rosebank contains not just oil but gas which would be piped to Shetland and on to the St Fergus terminal in Aberdeenshire, with the potential to heat 500,000 British homes at peak production.
Approval of this project, argues McCulloch, could pave the way for four more Jackdaw-sized gas developments in the waters west of Shetland – Tornado, Tornado East, Tobermory and Suilven.
"We would like to proceed with them," he said.
A surge in fossil fuel production if Rosebank is approved is exactly what campaigners fear.
It would, argues Tessa Khan, exacerbate the deadly and damaging impact of climate change for British teachers, nurses, firefighters and families worried about their children while making "huge profits for companies that are already incredibly profitable".
The oil from Rosebank would be loaded onto tankers via a gigantic hose and nozzle
When it comes to the impending UK government decision – which sources have told BBC News should come before Christmas – there is a strange mood at Rosebank.
The decision in favour of Jackdawhas clearly encouraged many on board but it has also highlighted the jeopardy they are facing.
For now, most workers we spoke to said they were just focusing on the job, with its strange rhythms and unusual restrictions – no ability to pop to the shops, no alcohol, a lot of special occasions missed.
And for some on board, very particular cravings.
For steward Liam Davidson, it is a desire to see his French bulldog, Bailey, at the end of his fortnight on board.
"My wee dog's at the heliport when I arrive," he said, "I do miss her."
It is hoped the decision on Rosebank will be made in the next few weeks
For Nicola Boyd, it's her double bed and a pizza delivery.
"I love seeing the family, but for me, it's the pizza," she told me.
But this time there might be a delay in delivering Boyd herself.
She is coming to the end of her fortnight but, as she helped us into our survival suits, the Met Office issued an amber weather warning for much of Scotland.
For Rosebank, it seems, there are stormy seas ahead, one way or the another.

title: How does the UK state pension compare with other countries?
summary: Do British pensioners have it better or worse than those in other countries?
body:
Getting older is something few of us want to think about. Yet how we fund our later years, and how much we'll get, has been a hot topic.
The triple lock formula - state pensions increasing by the greatest of 2.5%, earnings growth, or inflation - means those benefits have risen far faster than the earnings of workers since its introduction in 2011.
But as housing costs have also been rising fast, pensioner poverty has actually increased slightly in the last decade.
Nevertheless, even if you take those costs into consideration, pensioners are less likely to be in relative poverty - that is, having to get by on less than 60% of the income of the typical household - than families with children or working-age people.
And funding the triple lock has already cost the state billions more than initially envisaged. With that cost set to balloon further, the debate over whether that is sustainable, or fair, has raged for a while.
Andy Burnhamintends to start a new systemin a few years, which would see the state pension increase by at least inflation or 2.5%, and remove the automatic annual link with average earnings. It will likely mean less generous increases, although it will keep track with earnings growth over the longer term.
But are pensioners being short-changed in other ways? How do we compare with other countries?
One way of measuring that is to look at how generous the typical pension is relative to workers' average earnings - the replacement rate.
The OECD considers the outlook for those born at the start of the millennium in different countries on average wages, and assumes the pension system as it existed in 2022 is in place.
On that basis, looking at the basic state pension, retirement benefits in the UK look low compared with other wealthy countries.
And that is even when you consider that our system compels workers to be automatically enrolled in occupational schemes.
If you consider both of those, then after tax, UK retirement benefits would be 54.2% of average UK earnings, compared with an average of 63.2% across wealthy countries.
Burnham vows to end existing pension triple lock in 2030 to help fund care
State pension likely to top £13,000 a year
What is the triple lock and why are people talking about it?
But then there is income from other occupational and personal pensions, which are more prevalent in the UK. Include those and the gap narrows.
However, that does also mean that those relying on just the state pension for their incomes are a fair bit worse off than many retired people elsewhere.
So does that make the case for boosting spending on public pensions in the UK?
Well, the amount spent on the state pension is set to top £150bn a year, the single most expensive benefit to fund.
But other figures from the OECD show that the UK state spends a lower amount on total retirement benefits, relative to the size of its economy, than the average wealthy country.
But there are two issues to consider.
Firstly, this is about political choices, and the UK chooses to dedicate larger amounts to items such as universal healthcare.
And secondly, with ageing populations, the OECD reckons the amount needed for pensions may be set to soar in many nations by 2060 (the exceptions largely being those that are deploying changes).
Its predictions for the UK are likely to rise by less under the revised triple lock system being put in place by Andy Burnham but it may still mean more borrowing.
As it is, £1 in every £13 the UK government spends is to pay the interest on existing debt. And countries with more generous pensions, such as Italy, have faced pressure to reform.
So in many ways, with auto-enrolment into workplace pensions, the UK appears to be ahead of the game in insisting on universal privately funded pensions for workers. But that system raises another issue: the gender pension gap.
The gender pension gap is the difference between the average pension income of men and women aged 65 and over, as a percentage of men's average pension income.
It found that the typical gap in most wealthy countries is around 22.8% in favour of men.
But in the UK women typically get a pension that is a third less than what a man gets - in the main, due to the reliance on private pensions - although it should be noted that the most recent data the OECD has for the UK is for 2021.
Women are more likely to have received lower pay over the course of their working lives, taken career breaks or worked part time. And the hit to pension pots can be stark.
So step back and look at the big picture and British pensioners - and those who have yet to retire - may feel others have it better elsewhere.
But the message from all of this isn't to dwell on outrage but to take action.
The state pension has become more generous over the years, but if you want to enjoy the same kind of retirement as those elsewhere, get saving.
That is - if you can, and if you haven't left it too late.

title: UK to invest £100m in 'world first' AI Biosecurity Lab
summary: The chancellor will unveil AI spending aimed at shoring up the UK's defences in Wednesday's Budget.
body:
The UK says it will establish a national AI Biosecurity Lab (AIBL) to help strengthen its defences against emerging biological threats.
As part of Wednesday's Budget, the government will commit £100m to establishing the new, "world first" institute with the support of leading AI firms.
The chancellor will also pledge millions of pounds in spending across a range of initiatives aimed at shoring up the UK's ability to respond to evolving cyber, biological and AI-enabled threats.
"AI will transform daily life: every firm, community, hospital, school, and every aspect of our economy can benefit," John Healey said.
"I understand and share the concerns of working people, so I am setting out a distinctively British approach to AI.
"One that doesn't leave workers behind and defends our national interest, while ensuring the benefits of AI-enabled growth are felt right across the country."
The full details about the role and remit of the new lab are yet to emerge.
But the AI Minister Kanishka Narayan said it would be a "major new global institution" that brings together "world-leading scientific expertise" to ensure the UK can safeguard its citizens and goals as AI develops.
"That means staying ahead of emerging threats, from cyber attacks to biological risks, while building more of the critical technology our security depends on," he said.
"By backing British science, advanced chips and our own AI companies, we can strengthen our national security, rebuild Britain's industrial strength and create good, skilled jobs across the country."
The AI Biosecurity Lab's creation will also be supported by leading AI developers, with OpenAI and Anthropic providing £200m worth of AI model credits that can be spent on the use of their models.
What is AI, how does it work and why are some people concerned about it?
Don't leave AI to tech bros and oligarchs, UK's AI minister says
The Chancellor's plans to boost AI spending will also see an additional £120m committed to the UK's AI Security Institute (AISI).
Established by the former Conservative government in 2023, the lab evaluates the risks of the most advanced and powerful models - and has been championed for its role in helping build a collaborative and open approach to AI testing.
The additional funding announced by the Chancellor will aim to help ensure the lab can continue its efforts and work, particularly amid growing calls for technical standards and guardrails for AI development.
It will come alongside a £60m investment in what it coined a "National Cyber Shield" which it said would use agentic AI to boost cyber-defences, and £70m funding towards a National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability (NERV) Centre.
This, it said, would harness AI tools to detect cyber vulnerabilities across the UK's critical infrastructure and economy.
It comes after the UK government revealed it wasamong organisations around the world to have taken some sites offlineas a precaution after critical flaws were surfaced in a popular programming language.
Researchers who helped surface the vulnerabilities in PHP - a popular server-side scripting language used in web development for decades - warned platforms which use it could be exposed to potential hacks.
There have been no reports of any successful exploits of the flaw, coined php2shell, so far.
But experts have warned that the incident shows how quickly and easily bugs which have lain long dormant may be surfaced - and potentially exploited - using AI.

title: Civil servant who juggled five jobs says he was 'surprised' to be charged with fraud
summary: Kashim Chowdhury denied being dishonest when not telling employers he had other jobs.
body:
Civil servant Kashim Chowdhury is accused of fraududlently earning more than £284,000 by juggling multiple public sector jobs.
A civil servant accused of fraudulently juggling multiple government jobs says he was ''surprised'' to have been charged with fraud.
Kashim Chowdhury told the jury at Southwark Crown Court he had not been dishonest in failing to tell his employers he had other government jobs.
"At that time I was just on auto pilot, I was like a robot, I was not thinking clearly," he said.
Chowdhury, 55, from east London, is accused of nine counts of fraud. He denies acting dishonestly or intending to make a dishonest gain.
Between 2020 and 2023 Chowdhury had eight overlapping public sector jobs. He was contractually obliged to work full time and was paid a full-time salary by each organisation. He is accused of fraudulently earning more than £284,000.
In March 2023 Chowdhury began working for the Home Office despite being under contract to work full time at the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra), the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), the Department for Business and Trade and the Food Standards Agency.
The court was told he started the Home Office job while on sick leave from three of his other jobs.
Prosecuting barrister Lucy Organ asked him: "If you were really sick for work, how were you able to start your work at the Home Office?"
Chowdhury  said: "I did not want this job at the Home Office, I was told there would be adequate support and I could work whatever hours I wanted to work."
Organ also asked why he did not submit a sick note to the Home Office "You were using these sick notes to be able to cope. It was all too much wasn't it?"
Chowdhury rejected the suggestion, adding: "I wanted to carry on working."
In May 2023, Chowdhury was contracted to work 183 hours a week, more than the number of hours in seven days.
He told the jury he agreed with his employers to work flexibly and that his work was project or output based. He said this was agreed "informally" via text messages but the phones used to send the texts had gone missing when his house was searched by investigators.
He said that to cope with the workload he would work from 07:00 on Saturdays and Sundays and not finish until 20:00 or 21:00.
Civil servant faked illness with make-up to juggle five jobs, court hears
Civil servant admits he 'made mistakes' juggling five government jobs
Organ asked him: "Wasn't that a bit much for you?"
"I was house bound, I was looking after my mum," he said.
The prosecution alleges Chowdhury managed to keep his overlapping jobs secret because he worked entirely remotely. He told his employers he was the sole carer for his elderly mother and the prosecution alleges he "exploited this opportunity".
His line manager at the UKHSA, Aleesha Adams, organised a video call with him in May 2023 to discuss his sick leave.
She previously told the court she was surprised when he logged on wearing white make-up because his name led her to expect to see an Asian man with darker skin.
She told the court that as the meeting went on the make-up started coming off his forehead. ''He was sweating, it was like rubbing off so it was darker underneath and darker on the neck."
But Chowdhury denied having worn make-up at the meeting
''That's a smear, I've never worn make-up in my life. At that particular time, I was suffering from anxiety and depression. I had already submitted my sick note, there was no need to put on make-up.''

title: White House lifts tariffs on some Canadian goods as midterm elections loom
summary: From 30 October, tariffs will be eased on some products, including certain machinery, and placed on others, such as carpets.
body:
Canada and the US are currently locked in a tit-for-tat trade war
The Trump administration is lifting some of its 50% tariffs on Canadian goods two weeks before the midterm elections, after a Republican candidate in a key US Senate race said she had lobbied for the change.
From 30 October, tariffs will be eased on products including "plywood sheets, some paper products, certain machinery and refrigeration equipment", the White House said on Friday.
Republican Senator Susan Collins, who is in a tight race to keep her seat in Maine, first announced the exemptions, saying they would help her state's agriculture industry.
The US imposed a 50% levy on $20bn (£15bn) worth of Canadian goods after trade talks between the two countries collapsed in August.
Canada has imposed a series of countermeasures in response to the US tariffs, which Prime Minister Mark Carney said were "necessary to protect our workers".
Last month, Carneymatched the US tariffs"dollar for dollar" after the breakdown in talks. Trump had imposed them for what he called "unequal treatment" of US car, dairy and alcohol exports.
The White House said that, while tariffs would be lifted from some items, including some packing crates and boxes, they would be introduced on other items such as carpets and "waste products".
It said the action reflected US President Donald Trump's "continued efforts to defend American workers and ensure fair trade".
Maine Senator Susan Collins is seeking to keep her seat in November's midterm elections
Trump "continues to address Canada's discriminatory treatment of US commerce", White House spokesman Matthew Middleton said.
Canada's internal trade minister Dominic LeBlanc said: "While we assess these latest steps, Canada stands ready to work constructively and in good faith towards a more mutually beneficial trading relationship that respects Canada's interests."
The White House's announcement comes less than a fortnight before the US midterm elections, which will determine whether Trump's Republican Party or Democrats will control Congress, impacting the remaining two years of his term.
Collins said she had repeatedly asked senior Trump officials for tariff relief and that she would "continue working directly with administration officials to seek additional relief and encourage a broader trade agreement with Canada, our neighbour, ally and largest trading partner".
The US-Canada trade war in 5 charts
She wrote on X that the tariff exemptions were on products that were "crucial to Maine's agricultural industries, including blueberry, potato, apple, and seaweed producers".
Collins' Democratic challenger, Troy Jackson, responded: "Trump's trade wars have made life harder and more expensive for Mainers. Susan Collins enabled this chaos, voted to confirm the people behind it and now wants credit for bringing a cup of water to put out the fire."
Maine borders the Canadian provinces New Brunswick and Quebec. Its economy, as well as that of other border states, is deeply linked to Canada and they have felt the effects of the months-long trade war.
Michigan lawmaker Mike Rogers, also a Republican, has called on Trump to end the standoff after spending months supporting the policy in recent advertisements airing in his trade-reliant state.
Also on Friday, Trump said Canada was "working very hard" on a ⁠trade ​deal with the US.
Carney, who has sought closer ties with Europe since the tariff war erupted, said that Canada was open to a mutually beneficial deal, but was willing to wait it out.
"We could sign it this afternoon if the US were there," he said on Friday, according to Canadian broadcaster CBC. "If it has to be months from now or longer than that, or another administration, before a proper deal comes into place, we will do that."
LeBlanc confirmed on Thursday that a delegation met members of the Canada-United States Economic Relations Advisory Committee - the ninth meeting since April 2026. The committee members discussed the ongoing impact of US tariffs in Canada.

title: Burnham suggests stocking up on tinned food and bottled water
summary: The prime ministers says unexpected events seem to be becoming more common and it was wise to prepare.
body:
'Be prepared': PM Andy Burnham suggests stocking up on basic food items
The prime minister has advised people to stock up on tinned food and bottled water in order to be prepared for emergencies.
With storms battering the UK, and in the wake of online disruption caused by a major security flaw, Andy Burnham said "unexpected events seem to be becoming more and more common".
The government has drawn up recommendations for households to have three days' worth of bottled water and tinned food to deal with a crisis such as a war, an online attack or a natural disaster.
Burnham added: "It's not about panicking... It's about just taking sensible measures to have enough in the house to tide you over should there be a difficult situation."
At Labour's conference last month, Housing Secretary Angela Raynerjoked that her emergency box,externalwould include a bottle of wine.
She said she'd include: "Mascara, concealer, I don't know, a bottle of Sauvignon Blanc, a tin of baked beans because you've gotta have some baked beans, and I like a good tin of custard as well so I think that'll keep me going for a while."
Asked whether he agreed with her, Burnham told BBC Radio 5 Live's Matt Chorley: "Well, I'm not sure a bottle of wine is your best first port of call if you're in a slightly crisis situation, but it probably helps when you've done the hard work.
"But I'll stick to the basics I think - I do like my beans, so I have plenty of those in the cupboard, and soup.
"I think those are the kind of things that I would recommend people to have, as well as Twiglets, I'm not sure I can get by for too long without those."
Last month, theNational Audit Office (NAO) warned Britain's food supply chain is at riskgiven the growing threat of cyber-attacks and the climate crisis and said the Department for Food, the Environment and Rural Affairs (Defra) had not done enough in recent years to improve supply chain resilience.
The chief executive of the Cold Chain Federation, which represents firms transporting temperature-controlled foods, also told the BBC the UK is being targeted by Russian cyber-hackers who "know that there are pinch points in the food supply system".
Speaking at a wildfire resilience summit in Liverpool, Burnham denied the government had failed to properly prepare, saying: "No, we're having the conversation with people about being better prepared because we're living in a world where unexpected events seem to be becoming more and more common.
"Obviously, weather events, and we're in a situation today where the UK is facing storms and obviously, we feel for the people without power in Cornwall right now.
"It is just having those supplies in the house to get you through those moments. So we are having that conversation about resilience."

A checklist drawn up by the government recommends having nine litres of water per person – enough for three days – along with non-perishable food such as tinned meat and vegetables or dried fruit.
The government suggests having an FM radio, either battery or wind-up. During a national crisis, the BBC would prioritise broadcasting news, as well as health and safety information. In the event of a severe power cut, FM radio will be the best way to receive these updates.
The list also suggests hand sanitiser, wet wipes and toiletries, food for any pets, supplies for any babies, a torch, blankets, a charged power bank for devices, cash in case payment systems collapse, a first aid kit and copies of important documents.
Earlier, Treasury minister James Murray told BBC Breakfast he has not yet followed the government's guidance on stockpiling supplies to prepare for a crisis.
He said he had a stockpile of coffee, but pointed out that neighbouring countries including Ireland, France and the Netherlands had given the same guidance "for quite a long time".
He added: "I'm not going to pretend I've followed all that advice myself yet."
Speaking on the same programme, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said she was "stocked up for the week at any time".
She said the previous Conservative government had issued similar advice on preparing for emergencies, but added: "What I'm more concerned about is that it doesn't look like [the government] are explaining what the risks we are under are, and what they are doing about the big things.
"Families can stock up but what's going on with defence, the cyber attacks, the hybrid warfare? The money to look after the country has not been forthcoming."

title: Trump says Burnham 'getting it done' after Jackdaw decision
summary: The US president has praised Burnham after the government allowed gas drilling in the North Sea's Jackdaw field.
body:
Donald Trump said Andy Burnham's decision on Jackdaw would "make the UK a very rich country"
US President Donald Trump has praised Prime Minister Andy Burnham for the UK government's decision to approve production from the North Sea's Jackdaw gas field.
He said he had spoken with Burnham, telling reporters on Friday that the decision would "make the UK a very rich country".
Trump said: "The other prime minister, the previous man, Starmer. He's a very nice man, but he never got it done, and this one is getting it."
The decision had been subject to intense debate around its environment and economic impact and came after years of legal challenges.
The Jackdaw platform is located east of Aberdeen
Burnham announced the decision to approve the drilling of the Jackdaw gas field earlier this week.
Jackdaw is situated 150 miles (241km) east of Aberdeen and is operated by Adura, a joint venture between Shell and Norwegian state energy firm Equinor.
Ministers said the first gas could be produced by the end of this month, helping heat millions of homes, and also announced the creation of a new energy wealth fund.
Environmental campaigners say the decision would hamper efforts to tackle climate change and make "no meaningful difference" to UK energy security.
Based on official forecasts for the amount of gas the UK will need over the next decade, that suggests Jackdaw has the potential to meet around 1.6% of total projected national gas demand between 2026 and 2036.
Operators say it could be connected to the Great British gas network within weeks and could produce gas for the next 11 years.
Trump responded to the decision on Friday, but appeared to confuse oil and gas.
He said: "They're opening up the North Sea oil. I've been after them to do that for two years."
Trump added: "Andy is getting it done, and I guess it's against the liberal principle, but he knows what's right. It's going to make UK a very wealthy country."
In a discussion on Friday, Burnham and Trump spoke about the decision to approve Jackdaw.
The two leaders "agreed on the significant benefits this will bring to the UK, boosting the economy and supporting jobs for British workers", a statement from Number 10 read.
It added that Trump and Burnham "welcomed the continued collaboration between UK and US companies, especially on nuclear power".
Earlier this week, on Wednesday, Trump said the decision was "great news for the wealth and prosperity" of the UK.
Writing on his Truth Social platform, Trump urged the UK to go "full blast" and called the North Sea "one of the greatest and most prosperous areas of oil in the world".
A decision is yet to be takenon whether production can begin at Rosebank, the UK's largest known untapped oil field, which is located off the coast of Shetland in the North Atlantic.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch accused the prime minister of "dithering" on Jackdaw and said a ban on new oil and gas licences should be repealed.
However, Burnham said her party had "messed up" the original decision by not giving any regard to climate obligations - things he said "have to be considered in the round".
Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said gas from Jackdaw would be in homes and businesses this month, but that it would not lower energy bills this winter.
She said the decision was "compatible" with legally binding climate commitments, adding:  "We remain resolute in ending new licences for oil and gas and achieving net zero by 2050."
Environmental groups have criticised the Jackdaw approval. Areeba Hamid, the co-executive director of Greenpeace, said it was "the wrong decision" in terms of lowering energy bills, providing energy security, and addressing climate change.
Meanwhile, Oxfam said the government had "drilled straight through the UK's climate commitments".
During their Friday talks, Trump and Burnham spoke about the Falkland Islands and the Sea Lion oilfield project, a joint venture between British and Israeli companies.
In September, the Argentinian government threatened to impose economic sanctions on firms exploiting oil close to the Falkland Islands, and earlier this month, itbegan legal action to stop the exploration of oil and gas fields.
Burnham raised the "economic consequences ofArgentina's coercive measures for the UK and USand reiterated the importance of respecting the Islanders' right to develop their natural resources", Downing Street said.
The two leaders also discussed Ukraine, with the prime minister underlining the importance for Ukraine "to have full access to Starlink so they can continue to defend themselves against Russia's full-scale invasion", according to Number 10.
Starlink technology is a satellite system owned by Elon Musk's SpaceX company which Ukraine has relied upon during the war.
In recent days,Ukraine has been recording issues with the network, according to sources within the defence ministry. This has affected the country's ability to use attack drones and co-ordinate defensive operations.
The Downing Street statement added: "The Prime Minister recognised the work of President Trump to bring Putin to the negotiation table and the leaders agreed to work together, alongside international partners to bring an end to the bloodshed."

title: Tory activist in 'contract killing broker' claim had worked for party HQ
summary: Jack Ross was contracted to do social media work for the party until earlier this year, the BBC has been told.
body:
Jack Ross (pictured) held the post of Chief Operations Officer at Turning Point UK, an offshoot of the US organisation
A former Tory activist who appeared to offer to "broker" the hiring of contract killers in an undercover film report previously worked for Conservative headquarters.
Jack Ross was contracted to do social media work for the party until earlier this year, the BBC has been told.
It comes after Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch referred to them as "shocking allegations", adding that she did not "believe that person is a member anymore".
A Conservative spokesman said Ross's party membership had "been suspended with immediate effect pending an investigation". It has reported that Ross said his words were not meant to be taken seriously.
Ross was paid to provide social media advice to the party for a brief period, the BBC has been told. He was never an employee or Conservative Campaign Headquarters pass holder.
However, he met Badenoch on several occasions as part of his role as chief executive of Turning Point UK, an offshoot of a right-wing American organisation.
Ross has also met several other right-wing politicians including the former Prime Minister Boris Johnson and Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader.
In undercover filming broadcast this week by Al Jazeera, Ross appears to offer to "broker" the services of contract killers.
The Al Jazeera report said its undercover journalist approached Ross in 2022 with a fictitious situation of a family business at risk of being taken over by a criminal gang.
Ross is alleged to have asked the undercover reporter what was needed from him, and listed violent options that could be bought including stabbing, shooting and killing.
Al Jazeera said Ross denied the finding "completely" and claimed everything he said to the reporter was not meant seriously.
Turning Point UK has been approached for comment.

title: Green councillors face Labour deadline to disown Zionism policy
summary: Green leaders have been given until Sunday to disown their party's "Zionism is racism" conference vote.
body:
Green leader Zack Polanski has faced criticism over his response to the Zionism motion
Labour is set to decide whether to end power-sharing with Green councillors after demanding they disown their party's policy that Zionism is a form of racism.
The BBC has been told Green groups have been given until Sunday to respond to the demand, after which Labour's ruling National Executive Committee (NEC) will decide whether the party will continue with local deals to share power.
Green groups in some areas have publicly stated they do not agree with the policy or have distanced themselves from it, reducing the likelihood the pacts will end.
But in other areas Green councillors are yet to specify where they stand on the issue, meaning local alliances appear more vulnerable to collapse.
The issue is the most acute in nine local authorities where Greens are key partners in power-sharing arrangements, such as making up majorities that enable budgets to be passed and policy decisions to be made.
These include Sheffield City Council, Warwick District Council and Lewes District Council, three authorities where Labour and the Greens are in direct coalition.
The other areas where the Greens play a key role are: West Oxfordshire District Council, Stafford Borough Council, Havant Borough Council, Broadland District Council, Derbyshire Dales District Council and Wealden District Council.
In other areas, Green councillors are not central to local alliances continuing to function. These include Runnymede Borough Council, where Green councillors have left the local ruling alliance folllowing Labour's ultimatum.
In some areas, such as Lewes, Wealden, Broadland, West Sussex and North Somerset, local Green groups have distanced themselves from their party's Zionism policy, or said they do not agree with it.
But other Green groups are yet to publicly respond to Labour's demands, meaning there is greater uncertainty over the future of their co-operation with the party.
In Stafford, the power-sharing arrangement means the Greens have one cabinet member on the authority, councillor Tony Pearce, who holds the climate change portfolio.
Councillor Pearce has been contacted for comment but has not yet responded.
The leader of the Stafford Green group, Doug Rouxel told the BBC they were "formulating a response" to Labour's letter which they would like to put to party members first.
Labour confirmed the if the Greens refused to reject the Zionism policy, a process would then be triggered to remove Pearce from his cabinet position in Stafford.
Elsewhere, the leader of the Labour group on the Green-led Lewes District Council has resigned from the party, following his own party's ultimatum.
Chris Collier, who has been contacted for comment, will now sit as an independent cabinet member on the Labour-Green alliance that was formed to run the council in May 2023.
The BBC has been told Collier did not agree with the tone of Labour's ultimatum to the Green Party over the Zionism policy.
The "Zionism is racism" motion was passed by members of the Green Party of England and Wales at its annual conference in Brighton last month.
The policy motion adopted by members said Zionism was an ideology that supported an "ethnonationalist Jewish state" that had led to the "disenfranchisement and destruction" of Palestinians.
It backed the creation of a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine", which includes modern-day Israel.
It has led to a backlash from Jewish groups, as well as criticism from senior Green figures, including four of its five MPs.
Green leader Zack Polanski, who skipped the conference vote to unsuccessfully campaign for election in a Westminster by-election, has said he wants to see the "imperfect" motion amended in future.
Labour councillors require the approval of the party's NEC before entering into local tie-ups.
According to the party's rulebook, local groups must also "stand down" from power-sharing arrangements when asked to do so by their regional office.
By contrast, the Green Party of England and Wales allows local groups to make the final decision on where and whether to share power locally.
A Green Party spokesperson said: "For the Labour government to conflate criticism of Israel with antisemitism is disappointing and wrong.
"Trying to tell local parties what to do and who they can work with is undemocratic."
